extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of The Spectator; readers interested in literature, morals, and conduct (early-18th-century literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Short-form critical remarks and moral commentary (Spectator essays) evaluating behavior, virtue, and specifically Book 10 of Milton's Paradise Lost — focusing on poetic qualities, characterization, use of allegory, and moral effects. Targets evaluation of poetic technique and public conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of Devotion (avoid ostentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ostentatious Behaviour is such an Offence to true Sanctity, that it disparages it, and makes Virtue not only unamiable, but also ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of the pretended Devotée: carrying a showy emblem (white shock-dog with bells), bringing an 'abridg'd Piece of Morality' to display, attending public amusements only to 'pray heartily' that nobody be hurt, covering her face and making ejaculations before a meal as public performance. The Sacred Writings abhor this conduct; such behaviour deters others from goodness and makes religion contemptible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypocrisy in religious life diminishes moral authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A Devotée is so far from promoting Goodness, that she deters others by her Example. Folly and Vanity in one of these Ladies, is like Vice in a Clergyman; it does not only debase him, but makes the inconsiderate Part of the World think the worse of Religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public displays of false sanctity not only harm the individual's moral worth but degrade the reputation of religion generally; therefore true piety should avoid affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty as evidence of true courage and magnanimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Xenophon: Modesty in looks among the Spartans was such that 'you might as soon have turned the eyes of a Marble Statue upon you as theirs' — this modesty, joined to magnanimity, influenced their Courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts contemporary London affectation ('blustering Airs, big Looks, and bold Fronts') with Spartan modesty; genuine courage is accompanied by modest behaviour, not by loud gestures or staring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smartness/affectation equals emptiness and invites ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: General Affectation of Smartness, Wit, and Courage leads to ridicule and petty mockery in society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: red breeches as a 'certain Sign of Valour', tripping a beggar on crutches to boast agility, stealing a cock of a squire's hat — these displays are posed for show and provoke scorn rather than genuine esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rule for responding to reproach (Epictetus)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Man reproaches thee for being Proud or Ill-natured, consider whether his Reproaches are true; if false, remember he reviles an Imaginary Being; if true, change thy conduct and his reproaches will naturally cease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-examination: accept and reform when justified; ignore groundless slander as directed at an imagined version of you. This is framed as a piece of fortitude necessary for peace in a society of wit and liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgiveness and forbearance as superior to satirical retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a particular Merit in suppressing vindictive replies to critics; letting drop Wrath and stifling Resentments is 'Great and Heroical.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author recounts burning a satiric piece he had begun and taking pleasure in suppressing epigrams and lampoons; praises authors (Monsieur Balzac example) who can bear undeserved reproach without resentment — this temper is admired more than any satirical reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't overreact to petty critics (Boccalini's traveller)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuing or attacking every small annoyance is futile; 'Had he pursued his Journey without taking notice of them, the troublesome Insects would have died of themselves in a very few Weeks.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel to ignore minor criticisms — the public irritation will abate if you do not feed it by angry responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest motive for moral action: desire to please God
rubrics_metrics.description: The noblest Motive for Action is to act for the Glory and Happiness of our Being — to act with a settled faith aiming for reward only in another World; this 'heroick' pitch of virtue is the highest incentive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that many hide self-love under pretence of disinterestedness; true Christian virtue includes bestowing unseen good, overlooking hatred, and not being revengeful — these are duties of a Christian and the most honourable motives for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic structure: variety of persons and ensemble closure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tenth Book of Paradise Lost 'has a greater variety of Persons in it than any other in the whole Poem' and functions 'like the last Act of a well-written Tragedy' where all concerned are drawn up before the Audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful concluding book/act gathers all parties and shows the influence of the action on each; variety of persons and their respective parts is a positive structural quality in epic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to source material can justify departures from poetic abundance
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton 'has rather chosen to neglect the Numerousness of his Verse, than to deviate from those Speeches which are recorded' in Scripture — i.e., he preserved the form of the scriptural speeches even at the cost of other poetic flourishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When epic poetry deals with sacred/scriptural material, fidelity to recorded speeches and doctrinal form may be preferable to adding ornamental verse; this restraint can be praiseworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Scriptural allusion woven poetically
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's 'infinite Allusions to Places of Scripture' that are 'of a Poetical Nature, and which are woven with great Beauty into the Body of this Fable' are singled out as marks of poetic excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allusions to scripture enhance the poem when they are apt and poetical; the reviewer selectively notes such allusions rather than cataloguing them all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character depiction: human persons should evoke pity and commiseration
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's representation of Adam and Eve is 'wonderfully contriv'd to influence the Reader with Pity and Compassion' — Adam's weakness is pardonable as human frailty and Eve's speeches are 'exquisitely moving and pathetick.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In an epic treating fall or tragedy, rendering protagonists with emotional depth and motives that elicit sympathy (even when their actions harm humanity) is a mark of skill; tender passages engage a broad readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginary persons/allegory: fine in short phrases, risky in sustained heroic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegorical Persons (like Sin and Death) are 'exquisite in their Kind, if not considered as a Part of such a Work' and Homer uses such figures acceptably in short expressions rather than in engaged series of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for epic composition: personifications and extended allegories can be beautiful but may be less appropriate when they become principal actors in a heroic poem; brevity or episodic use is safer and more classical (Homer/Virgil examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation and grand scenic invention as epic virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's description of Satan's transformation and the 'unexpected Hiss' and 'Dimensions and Bulk of Satan' that change into different forms is praised as an instance of 'delightful Surprize' and 'Beauty of the Diction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic episodes that provide imaginative surprises, large-scale transformations, and finely judged diction contribute to the poem's excellence; the craft in finishing incidental scenes is especially notable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification and figurative economy as effective poetic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Using personification as brief poetic shorthand (e.g., 'Victory sat on the right Hand of the Messiah', 'Discord as the Mother of Funerals') conveys thought pleasingly and is distinguished from long allegorical treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise personifications and figures of speech that convey common ideas vividly; such 'poetical Phrases' are apt where sustained allegory would be inappropriate.
